text: Chemo- and Regioselective Palladium-Catalyzed Internal Hydrosilylation of gem-Difluoroallenes to Access β‑Fluorinated Vinylsilanes
Xin-Long Yu, An-Jiu Wen, Zheng Xu, Samuel Couve-Bonnaire,\* Li-Wen Xu,\* and Jean-Philippe Bouillon\*
KEYWORDS: gem-difluoroallene, vinylsilane, palladium, catalysis, hydrosilylation

difluoroallenes, providing straightforward access to valuable gem-difluorovinylsilanes. The reaction proceeds with excellent regio- and chemoselectivity under mild conditions, demonstrating remarkable potential for late-stage functionalization applications. Through comprehensive Density Functional Theory (DFT) studies, we have elucidated the critical role of the DPEphos ligand in facilitating the internal hydrosilylation of gem-difluoroallenes, ofering mechanistic insights into the control of reaction selectivity. This novel approach to selective gem-difluoroallene transformation enables the synthesis of previously inaccessible gem-difluorovinylsilanes, which serve as versatile building blocks for diverse chemical transformations.

The fluorine atom is considered to significantly alter the physicochemical properties of drug molecules due to its high electronegativity and small size.<sup>1</sup> Additionally, the introduction of fluorine-containing groups could enhance the lipophilicity, metabolic stability, and membrane permeability of the molecules, thereby improving their eficacy and pharmacokinetic properties.<sup>2</sup> In recent years, gem-difluoroalkenes have attracted much attention in the field of medicinal chemistry<sup>3</sup> as a bioisostere of carbonyl group, which could efectively improve the metabolic stability of molecules and optimize the biological activity by modulating the electronic properties of the target binding sites.<sup>4</sup> For instance, the replacement of the carbonyl group in the artemisinin molecule by a gemdifluoroalkene moiety significantly enhanced the antimalarial activity, suggesting that its structure showed efects on the interaction of the molecule with the biological targets based on the adjustment of the electronic distribution and spatial conformation. Furthermore, the gem-difluoroalkene moiety exhibited unique electronic properties and could be employed in the regulation of the lipophilicity and metabolic stability of molecules, alongside the design of more selective targeted drugs making it a versatile module in drug design (Scheme 1A).<sup>5</sup>

Diferent from the typical allenes, gem-difluoroallenes possessed the unique backbone of 1,2-propadiene with two fluorine atoms at the terminal position. The electronwithdrawing efect of fluorine atoms showed significant efects on the reactivity of gem-difluoroallenes.<sup>6</sup> Moreover, due to its high electronegativity and strong C−F bond, the electrophilic α-carbon is more favorable to react with nucleophilic reagents. Although fluorine is not generally considered as a good leaving group, it can often be easily dissociated from gem-difluorinated olefins or activated alkyl fluoride groups under strongly nucleophilic or alkaline conditions.<sup>7</sup> Compared with the α- and γ-selective additions to gem-difluoroallene, β-addition reactions are relatively rare. In 2022, Shi’s group reported the selective β-addition of thiols to gem-difluoroallenes by a rhodium catalyst, in which the β-adducts were obtained in fair to good yields (58−77%) with high chemo- and regioselectivity (up to 20:1 rr) leading to thioenolether with the difluoromethyl group in allylic position.<sup>8</sup> It was revealed by mechanistic studies that the reaction proceeded through a stable Z-rhodacyclic transition state, which enabled precise control over β-selectivity. However, to our knowledge, this is the only example reported achieving β-additions on gem-

Although numerous studies have documented the addition reactions of various hydrogen-functionalized compounds $( \mathrm { e . g . } ,$ C−H, N−H, O−H, S−H, and P−H bonds) to gemdifluoroallenes (Scheme 1B),<sup>10−13</sup> t he hydrosilylation of gemdifluoroallenes remains unexplored. Notably, existing methods predominantly aford α-functionalized products, whereas regioselective β-position addition to access gem-difluorovinyl compounds remains a significant challenge. Additionally, while hydrosilylation reactions of terminal alkenes are welldeveloped,<sup>14</sup> the corresponding transformations of internal alkenes are far less explored. This discrepancy arises from the higher reactivity and lower steric hindrance of terminal alkenes, which facilitate eficient coordination with metal catalysts and promote hydrosilylation. Moreover, controlling the regioselectivity of internal alkene hydrosilylation remains a critical challenge in this field (Scheme 1C).<sup>15</sup> To the best of our knowledge, only two examples of internal allene hydrosilylation have been reported,<sup>16</sup> in stark contrast to the well-established hydrosilylation of terminal allenes.<sup>17</sup>

Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed chemo- and regioselective hydrosilylation of gem-difluoroallenes, providing eficient access to β-difluorovinylsilanes under mild conditions (Scheme 1D). This method ofers a new strategy for constructing difluorovinylsilanes and difluorovinyl-containing organic molecules.

The gem-difluoroallene (1a) and diphenylsilane (2a) were used as model substrates to optimize the reaction. During the initial screening experiments, ${ \bar { \mathrm { P d } } } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) _ { 2 }$ was employed as the catalyst with toluene as the solvent at room temperature, in order to evaluate the performance of various ligands. Triphenylphosphine $\left( \mathrm { P P h } _ { 3 } \right)$ produced trace amounts of the desired target product 3a (Table 1, entry 1). Notably, the yield showed an increasing trend to 57% with the use of triphenylphosphite (TPP) as the ligand (Table 1, entry 2).

text: In contrast, nitrogen-based bidentate ligand (Bpy), bidentate phosphine ligand (DPPE), and ferrocenyl-based ligand (DPPF) were inefective for the desired hydrosilylation (Table 1, entries 3−5). Among other bidentate-phosphine ligands, BINAP resulted in a modest yield of 18% (Table 1, entry 6), while Xantphos showed a slightly better performance with a yield of 32% (Table 1, entry 7). Notably, [2- (diphenylphosphino)phenyl] ether (DPEphos) achieved a higher yield of 64% of the desired gem-difluorovinylsilane 3a (Table 1, entry 8). For further improvement of the yield of this reaction, the efect of solvents including dichloromethane (DCM), hexane, THF, EtOAc, and 1,4-dioxane was evaluated. It was found that ether-based solvents showed better activity than other solvents, in which the best results were obtained with 1,4-dioxane leading to 98% of the NMR yield of the target product (Table 1, entries 9−13). Notably, the product revealed to be unstable during long purification over silica gel column chromatography, requiring rapid purification to achieve high yields. However, once isolated, it remains stable. Additionally, the evaluation of various palladium catalysts was conducted in this study, in which $\mathrm { P d } ( \bar { \mathrm { O A c } } ) _ { 2 }$ showed the best catalytic performance, whereas other palladium catalysts such as $\mathrm { \dot { P d } _ { 2 } ( \dot { d b } a ) _ { 3 } { \cdot } C H C l _ { 3 } , \Delta \ P d ( P P h _ { 3 } ) _ { 4 } , }$ and $\mathrm { P d B r } _ { 2 }$ exhibited significantly lower or no activity (Table 1, entries 14−16). Overall, it was demonstrated by the optimization of the catalyst loading that the reaction could be achieved with only 2 mol % of $\mathrm { P d } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) _ { 2 }$ and 3 mol % of DPEphos (Table 1, entry 17).

The substrate scope of gem-difluoroallenes (1a) with various silanes (2a−k) was then investigated under the optimized reaction conditions (Scheme 2). The results showed that a range of diarylsilanes eficiently reacted with gem-difluoroallenes in the current system, exhibiting excellent chemo- and regioselectivity and yielding products 3 in moderate to excellent yields. The scope was composed of diarylsilanes with neutral substituents (2a), electron-donating substituents (2b−e), and a halogen atom (2f) leading to corresponding products 3a−f with yields ranging from 56 to 90%. Arylalkylsilanes with diferent alkyl groups, such as methyl (2g), CH TMS (2h), and tert-butyl (2i, 2j), could also aford the target products 3g−j in high yields, indicating that increased steric hindrance showed no significant efects on the reaction yield and β-selectivity. Notably, the relatively lower isolated yields observed for certain arylalkylsilanes (2g− 2j) are likely due to the instability of the corresponding hydrosilylation products on silica gel, which can lead to partial desilylation during purification. In contrast, products derived from diarylsilanes exhibited higher stability under the same conditions, thus enabling better yields after chromatographic separation. This observation highlights the diferent behaviors of arylalkylsilanes and diarylsilanes in the reaction and purification processes. Additionally, phenylsilane 2k also showed good activity within this reaction delivering the corresponding product 3k in 52% yield. In addition, under conditions involving excess $\mathrm { P h } S \mathrm { i H } _ { 3 } ,$ the bis-hydrosilylation product (3l) was successfully obtained, and the monohydrosilylation product (3k) was not detected. This experiment indicates distinct diferences in reactivity among diferent hydrosilanes and suggests a sequential addition process.

Additionally, a substrate with −OBn substituents also showed good tolerance under these experimental conditions with phenyl tert-butylsilane furnishing the corresponding product 3t in a fair 50% yield. Regarding the disubstituted aryl substrates $( 2 , 4 \mathrm { - C l } _ { 2 } , \ 3 , 4 \mathrm { - M e } _ { 2 } )$ , the reaction yielded 3r and 3s products with 52% and 82% yields, respectively, and the more polar substituents (−OMe, − $\mathbf { C O } _ { 2 } \mathbf { M e } )$ were also well-tolerated leading to the products 3u and 3v in 76% and 79% yields, respectively.

gem-Difluoroallenes containing heterocycles (furan, thiophene, 2,3-dioxane) exhibited good to excellent reactivity under these reaction conditions leading to the corresponding products $3 \mathbf { w } - 3 \mathbf { y }$ in yields ranging from 71 to 92%. Furthermore, substrates containing chlorine, tert-butyldiphenylsilyl (TBDP) ether terminal alkenes, and long alkyl chains also reacted successfully furnishing the corresponding products 3z−3ac, with yields ranging from 62% to 74%. Notably, tetrasubstituted gem-difluoroallene also showed high eficiency in the reaction, with the target product 3ad obtained in 81% yield, albeit without diastereoselectivity (dr value of 1:1). The broad substrate compatibility and excellent regioselectivity were demonstrated in this reaction system based on the above results, which could efectively accommodate various silanes and gem-difluoroallenes, and it could provide an eficient synthetic strategy for the construction of functionalized silanes and complex organic molecules. Additionally, these findings could further highlight the potential applications of this reaction and provide valuable insights into the development of gem-difluorovinyl chemistry. To further demonstrate the viability of our reaction, gem-difluoroallene from citronellal was successfully employed in this study, and the product 3ae was obtained in 92% yield with complete regioselectivity.

Gram-scale reactions of substrate 1a were successfully conducted with diphenylsilane 2a and phenylsilane 2k and provided 1.12 g of product 3a (60% yield) and 0.87 g of product 3k (60% yield) with maintained high chemo- and regioselectivity. We further employed both products to demonstrate the versatile transformation potential of the gem-difluorovinylsilanes. From 3a, hydrogenation under Pd/C in $\mathrm { T H F } / \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ as a solvent aforded silanol 4 in 90% yield, while methanol as a solvent aforded silyl ether 5 in 92% yield. Additionally, treatment with $\mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \dot { \mathrm { I } _ { 2 } } / \mathrm { E t } _ { 2 } \mathrm { Z n }$ produced alkylsubstituted silane 6 in 70% yield. The hydrosilylation of diphenylacetylene under $\mathrm { P d } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) _ { 2 } / \mathrm { P P h } _ { 3 }$ catalysis with 3k aforded the vinylation product 7 in 72% yield. In addition, cyclization of 3k with 1,4-butanediol under ${ \mathrm { C s } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { C O } } _ { 3 }$ catalysis formed cyclic dioxasilolane 8 in 75% yield (Scheme 4A). The comparison between branched product 9 from nonfluorinated allene and our difluoroallene products 3 could suggest that the fluorine’s electron-withdrawing efect governed the regiocontrol of the reaction (Scheme 4B). A deuterium labeling experiment with substrate 1a and $\mathrm { P h } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i D } _ { 2 }$ (2a-D) demonstrated >99% of D-incorporation in vinylsilane 3a-D (Scheme 4C), while kinetic isotope experiments (KIE = 1) seemed to exclude Si−H/D bond cleavage as the ratedetermining step (Scheme 4D).

Building upon previous reports of Pd-catalyzed hydrosilylation<sup>15a,18</sup> a nd guided by our control experiments, we conducted a systematic mechanistic investigation using density functional theory (DFT) calculations with gem-difluoroallene (1a) and diphenylsilane (2a) as model substrates (Scheme 5).

Combining experimental and computational insights, we elucidated the selective formation of major product 3a in a Pd/DPEphos-catalyzed system. As shown in Scheme $5 ,$ the proposed catalytic cycle involves several key steps. Initially, the palladium precursor is reduced in situ by the phosphine ligand to generate the active Pd(0)Ln species (denoted as PdL), which serves as the reference point $\left( \Delta G = 0 \right)$ for the Gibbs free energy profile. While palladium typically favors coordination with terminal alkenes, the electron-withdrawing efect of the fluorine substituents in 1a shifts the preference to the internal ${ \mathrm { C } } _ { 2 } { = } { \mathrm { C } } _ { 3 }$ double bond, forming intermediate A. DFT calculations confirmed that coordination at the distal double bond $\left( \mathbf { C } _ { 2 } { = } \mathbf { C } _ { 3 } \right)$ is energetically favored by 11.8 kcal/mol over the proximal $\mathrm { C } _ { 1 } { = } \mathrm { C } _ { 2 }$ bond. Subsequent oxidative addition of the Si−H bond in 2a to A yields complex B, which undergoes migratory insertion of the olefin into the Pd−H bond, afording the silyl alkyl Pd(II) intermediate C. Four distinct transition states (TS1-1, TS1-3, TS1-5, and TS1-7) were located along pathways 1, 3, 5, and 7, respectively. This insertion step was identified as the rate-determining step (RDS), critically governing both the reactivity and regioselectivity. Comparative analysis of the two competing pathways, as H-insertion versus Si-insertion, revealed that the former consistently exhibits lower activation barriers (see Supporting Information). Finally, reductive elimination from C generates complex D, which releases the product and regenerates PdL to close the catalytic cycle. Energetically, the H-insertion pathway followed by reductive elimination proved to be the most favorable, with TS1-1 exhibiting the lowest activation barrier (17.6 kcal/mol), consistent with the experimental predominance of 3a. Intriguingly, despite minimal energy diferences between TS1-1 and TS1-3, the preferential coordination of Pd to the distal double bond $\left( \mathbf { C } _ { 2 } { = } \mathbf { C } _ { 3 } \right)$ drives the selectivity toward 3a. In contrast, TS1-5 displayed the highest barrier (22.5 kcal/mol), attributed to the electron-withdrawing fluorine substituents, which render the γ-position less nucleophilic by inductively stabilizing a partial positive charge at the α-carbon. Notably, even in the absence of fluorine substituents (e.g., with hydrogen at the α-position), the Hinsertion pathway remains energetically favored, though the product distribution shifts to the branched allylic silane 9 (see Supporting Information).

text: In summary, we have developed a novel palladium-catalyzed β- selective hydrosilylation of gem-difluoroallenes with hydrosilanes, providing eficient access to gem-difluorovinylsilanes. This method exhibits a broad substrate scope, delivering the target products in moderate to excellent yields, and demonstrates excellent compatibility with late-stage functionalization strategies. Mechanistic investigations through density functional theory (DFT) calculations revealed the key transition states, ofering fundamental insights into the origin of the observed chemo- and regioselectivity. Given the mild reaction conditions and operational simplicity of this protocol, the resulting β-difluorovinylsilanes and their derivatives hold significant potential for diverse applications in synthetic chemistry and pharmaceutical research.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of gem-Difluoroallenes 1. To a solution of (i-Pr) NH (20 mmol) in THF (10 mL) was added n-BuLi (20.0 mmol) over 10 min at $0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ under argon. The resulting solution was allowed to stir for an additional 15 min and then cooled to $- 8 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ in a cold ethanol bath. To the cold LDA solution was added a solution of $\mathrm { C F } _ { 3 } \mathrm { C H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { I }$ (10.0 mmol) in THF (5 mL) over 10 min, keeping the temperature between $- 9 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and $- 8 5 ~ ^ { \circ } C .$ After the mixture was stirred for 20 min at that same temperature, a solution of aldehyde (10.0 mmol) in THF (5 mL) was added over 5 min, keeping the temperature between $- 9 3 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and −85 $^ \circ \mathrm { C } .$ The mixture was stirred for an additional 30 min, then warmed $\mathrm { t o } - 3 0 \ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ over 90 min. After $\mathtt { A c } _ { 2 } \mathtt { O }$ (12.0 mmol) was added, the mixture was allowed to warm to $0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ over 2 h. The reaction was quenched with sat. aq $\mathrm { N H } _ { 4 } \mathrm { C l }$ (20 mL), and the products were extracted with ethyl acetate $( 3 \times 2 0 ~ \mathrm { m L } )$ . The combined organic layer was washed with brine (20 mL) and dried $\left( \mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 } \right)$ . After the solvent was removed under reduced pressure, the residue was purified by flash column chromatography giving acetate S1 (see Supporting Information). To a suspension of zinc powder (17.0 mmol) in DMF (26 mL) was added a solution of S1 (8.50 mmol) in DMF (17 mL) at room temperature under argon, and the mixture was stirred for 3 h. The resulting mixture was filtered to remove the excess zinc and then diluted with ethyl acetate (20 mL) and brine (15 mL). The products were extracted with ethyl acetate $( 3 \times 1 5$ mL). The combined organic layer was washed with brine (15 mL) and dried $\left( \mathrm { N a } _ { 2 } S \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } \right)$ . After the solvent was removed under reduced pressure, the residue was purified by flash column chromatography (pentane) to give compound 1.

text: General Procedure for the Synthesis of gem-Difluorovinylsilanes 3. A Schlenk tube was purged with argon three times, and to the tube were added $\mathrm { P d } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) .$ <sub>2</sub> (0.9 mg, 2 mol %), DPEphos (3.2 mg, 3 mol %), and $^ { 1 , 4 }$ -dioxane (2 mL) under an argon atmosphere. Then, 1,1-difluoroallene 1 (0.2 mmol, 1.0 equiv) and silane 2 (0.24 mmol, 1.2 equiv) were added subsequently. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 h. The resulting mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure, and the residue was purified by flash column chromatography on silica gel to aford the difluorovinylsilanes 3.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of (1,1-Difluoro-5-phenylpent-1-en-2-yl)diphenylsilanol 4. A solution of 3a (72.8 mg, 0.2 mmol) in THF (2.0 mL, containing 1% v/v H O) was added to a flame-dried Schlenk tube under argon, and Pd/C (15.0 mg, 10 wt %) was added and stirred at room temperature. After the reaction was completed (10 min), DCM (5.0 mL) was added and dried by ${ \bf N a } _ { 2 } { \bf S O } _ { 4 } ;$ then the reaction mixture was filtered through a pad of Celite, eluted with ethyl acetate, concentrated in vacuo, and purified by silica gel chromatography (pentane:EA = 100/0 to 95/5) to give the product 4.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of (1,1-Difluoro-5-phenylpent-1-en-2-yl)(methoxy)diphenylsilane 5. A solution of 3a (72.8 mg, 0.2 mmol) in MeOH (2.0 mL) was added to a flame-dried Schlenk tube under argon, Pd/C (15.0 mg, 10 wt %) was added, and the mixture was stirred at room temperature. After the reaction was completed, DCM (5.0 mL) was added and dried by ${ \mathrm { N a } } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 } ;$ then the reaction mixture was filtered through a pad of Celite, eluted with ethyl acetate, concentrated in vacuo, and purified by silica gel chromatography (pentane:EA = 100/0 to 98/2) to give the product 5.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of (1,1-Difluoro-5-phenylpent-1-en-2-yl)(methyl)diphenylsilane 6. A solution of 3a (72.8 mg, 0.2 mmol) in DCE (2.0 mL) was added to a flame-dried Schlenk tube under argon; CH I (16.0 eq, 3.2 mmol) and Et Zn (8.0 eq, 1.6 mmol) were added and stirred at room temperature. After the reaction was completed, DCM (5.0 mL) was added and dried by ${ \bf N a } _ { 2 } { \bf S O } _ { 4 } ;$ then the reaction mixture was filtered through a pad of Celite, eluted with ethyl acetate, concentrated in vacuo, and purified by silica gel chromatography to give the product 6.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of (E)-(1,1- Difluoro-5-phenylpent-1-en-2-yl)(1,2-diphenylvinyl)- (phenyl)silane 7. In a flame-dried Schlenk tube, were added Pd(OAc) (0.9 mg, 2 mol %), PPh (2.1 mg, 4 mol %) in cyclohexane (1 mL, 0.2 M). Then, 3k (57.7 mg, 0.2 mmol) and diphenylacetylene (45.2 mg, 0.2 mmol) were added sequentially to the reaction mixture, and the reaction tube was cooled at room temperature and then stirred for 12 h. After completion of the reaction, the mixture was passed through a short Celite pad, using DCM as a solvent. The residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel to aford the corresponding product 7 as a colorless oil.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of 2-(1,1- Difluoro-5-phenylpent-1-en-2-yl)-2-phenyl-1,3,2-dioxasilepane 8. Inside a nitrogen-atmosphere glovebox, $\mathrm { C s } _ { 2 } \mathrm { C O } _ { 3 }$ (0.02 mmol, 10 mol %, 6.6 mg) was charged into an ovendried 10 mL Schlenk tube equipped with a stirring bar. The reaction tube was capped tightly and removed from the glovebox. Subsequently, silane 3k (0.2 mmol, 1.0 equiv, 57.7 mg) and 1,4-butanediol (0.24 mmol, 1.2 equiv, 43.2 mg) and THF (3.0 mL) were added under an argon atmosphere and then stirred at room temperature for 3 h. Then the mixture was diluted and extracted with DCM. The organic layer was washed with brine, dried with anhydrous ${ \mathrm { N a } } _ { 2 } S { \mathrm { O } } _ { 4 } ,$ filtered, and concentrated in vacuo. The residue was purified by column chromatography on silica gel to aford the corresponding product 8 as a colorless oil.

General Procedure for the Synthesis of Diphenyl(5- phenylpent-1-en-3-yl)silane 9. The Schlenk tube was purged with argon three times, and to the tube were added $\mathrm { P d } ( \mathrm { O A c } ) _ { 2 }$ (0.9 mg, 2 mol %), DPEphos (3.2 mg, 3 mol %), and 1,4-dioxane (2 mL) under an argon atmosphere. Then, allene (0.2 mmol, 1.0 equiv) and $\mathrm { P h } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S i H } _ { 2 }$ (0.24 mmol, 1.2 equiv) were added subsequently. The reaction mixture was stirred at room temperature for 12 h. The resulting mixture was concentrated under reduced pressure, and the residue was purified by flash column chromatography on silica gel to aford the difluorovinylsilanes 9.
